lesson.title: Madison and Jefferson Answer the Sedition Act in Secret
lesson.summary: Written secretly by Madison and Jefferson in 1798, the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions argued that states could judge the constitutionality of federal laws, planting a states' rights theory that outlived the Alien and Sedition Acts by decades.
lesson.body:
In the fall of 1798, alarmed by the Alien and Sedition Acts and unable to challenge them through the Federalist controlled Congress or the Federalist leaning federal courts, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison turned to state legislatures instead. Working quietly and without publicly attaching their names to the documents, Jefferson drafted a set of resolutions adopted by the Kentucky legislature in November 1798, while Madison drafted a similar set adopted by Virginia's legislature in December of that year.

Both sets of resolutions rested on what is often called compact theory, the idea that the Constitution was fundamentally an agreement among sovereign states, which had created the federal government and delegated it only specific, limited powers. Since the Alien and Sedition Acts, in Jefferson and Madison's view, exceeded those delegated powers and violated the First Amendment protections found in the Bill of Rights, the resolutions argued that the laws were void and that states had both the right and the duty to declare unconstitutional federal laws invalid when Congress overstepped.

Jefferson's Kentucky Resolutions went further than Madison's Virginia version, using the word interposition and, in a follow up resolution passed in 1799, explicitly raising the idea that states could nullify federal laws they judged unconstitutional within their own borders. Madison's Virginia Resolutions were somewhat more cautious, describing interposition as a check that states could invoke to draw public attention to federal overreach rather than a specific mechanism for nullifying laws outright.

The resolutions were a direct application of the federalism established by the Constitution, testing the boundary between state and national authority that had already been debated in disputes like the national bank fight, but pushing that argument into genuinely new territory by suggesting individual states might refuse to enforce a federal law. No other state legislatures endorsed the resolutions at the time, and several northern states passed responses rejecting the idea that states could unilaterally nullify federal law, leaving Kentucky and Virginia isolated in the moment.

Even though they had little immediate legal effect, the resolutions had a long afterlife. They articulated a theory of states' rights and nullification that reappeared throughout the nineteenth century, most famously when South Carolina cited similar reasoning during the nullification crisis of the early 1830s and again in arguments over slavery and secession before the Civil War. In their own moment, the resolutions functioned mainly as political documents, rallying opposition to the Federalists and helping set the stage for the election of 1800, in which the Alien and Sedition Acts became one of the central issues voters weighed against Adams and his party.
